newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese need permit to visit HK before handover.
newsitem.headline: Chinese need permit to visit HK before handover.

text.p: China has issued tighter rules on already restricted travel to Hong Kong to prevent a flood of visitors eager to witness Beijing's historic resumption of sovereignty over the British colony, officials said on Monday.

"The reason why we limited people from the mainland going to Hong Kong is that Hong Kong is too small to receive the number of people who want to witness Hong Kong's return," an official of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office said.
The restrictions would be in place from June 15 to July 15 while transit stopovers would be banned from June 30 to July 2.
"People from mainland China are not allowed to go to Hong Kong from June 15 to July 15," an official of the Hong Kong Handover Information Centre told Reuters.
Travel agents said they had received an official directive to issue plane tickets to Hong Kong only to Chinese who have obtained special permits to make such visits.
However, flights would remain unchanged despite the tighter restrictions with many Chinese officials and businessmen expected to travel to the territory during the handover.
"All flights to Hong Kong will remain as usual," an official of the Civil Aviation Administration of China said.
China resumes sovereignty over Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, bringing to an end more than 150 years of British colonial rule over the booming city.

The handover of Hong Kong has been met with widespread excitement from most Chinese, with many eager to see for themselves the territory's economic miracle but unaware that currently tight travel restrictions will remain in place after Beijing resumes sovereignty.

China's resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong will make it no easier for Chinese to obtain permission to enter the territory since its system is to remain unchanged for 50 years in line with Sino-British treaties governing the handover.

To try to stem the anticipated flood of eager mainland Chinese sightseers during the handover, the British embassy in Beijing has stopped handling visa applications from holders of private Chinese passports, British sources said.
Visas for Chinese with official passports would be processed up to the handover, a British source said, adding that the number of such applicants had risen as the handover date neared.
"The British embassy has already stopped issuing visas to Chinese who want to go to Hong Kong during this period," the information centre official said.

After July 1, Chinese wanting to visit Hong Kong will have to apply to immigration authorities in the territory for the necessary permission, and Hong Kong officials were now negotiating with China to set up an office in Beijing that could handle such applications, officials said.

China is organising hundreds of official and semi-official events to celebrate the handover, hailed by its communist leadership as one of the key events of 1997 and a major milestone in Chinese history.

Hundreds of Chinese excited about the recovery of Hong Kong packed the grounds of a former imperial summer palace near Beijing late on Sunday to watch the lights go on in a huge cardboard model of Hong Kong -- the closest they will come to seeing the territory.

"This period in history, including the loss of Hong Kong, is a disgrace to the Chinese people," said student Lu Shasha, who visited the lantern show amid the ruins of the summer palace burnt down by invading British troops in 1860. "The handover demonstrates that China is more powerful now than before."
